transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, hello doctor. Thank you for seeing me. You know, I wasn't entirely sure if I should come in at first, because it feels like such a silly thing to bother a doctor with, but things are just... well, what made me actually pick up the phone and come in today is that my eating has gotten all turned around. Just completely upside down. 

It's the strangest thing, really. Some days, I'll just be sitting in my living room, maybe watching a program or just looking out the window, and I'll glance over at the clock and it's suddenly three or four in the afternoon, and I realize I forgot lunch completely. It just slips right out of my mind, which isn't like me at all. I've always been a strict three-meals-a-day sort of person, ever since I was a little girl. You know how it was back then, you sat at the table when it was time. 

But then, on the other days, it's the exact opposite. I'll find myself just wandering into the kitchen and standing right there at the counter—not even sitting down at the table properly like a civilized person—just standing there eating crackers and sweets. I'll go through a whole sleeve of saltines or those little cookies I keep in the tin. And the most frustrating part of the whole ordeal is that nothing even tastes right. It's like I'm chewing on dust or cardboard, there's just no joy in it at all, but I just keep standing there eating anyway. I don't know why I do it, but my whole routine is just entirely thrown off, and I just don't know what to make of it anymore.
Have you been feeling down or losing interest in things you usually enjoy?

Well, yes... I suppose that's exactly it. It's hard to admit, really, because I've always been someone who tries to look on the bright side of things. My late husband always used to say I was the optimist of the family, always finding the silver lining. But lately... goodness me, it's just been so terribly difficult to find any silver linings anywhere. 

Most mornings now, I just wake up and there's this... this awful, heavy, low feeling sitting right on my chest. I'll just lie there under the quilt, looking up at the ceiling, and it feels like all the color has just completely gone out of the day before I even manage to get myself dressed. And getting dressed used to be such a nice little routine for me, you know? Picking out a nice blouse, making sure I looked presentable even if I was just staying in the house. Now I just sit on the edge of the mattress and think, well, what's the point? The whole day just stretches out in front of me looking so gray and dull. 

I used to love my morning crossword puzzles, or tending to my African violets in the sunroom—I've had some of those plants for over a decade, if you can believe it, grown them right from little cuttings—but lately, I just walk right past them. I look at the things I used to love doing and I just feel... nothing. No interest at all. I haven't even picked up my knitting needles in weeks. It's just that awful, sinking heaviness from the very moment I open my eyes, and I just can't seem to shake it off, no matter how hard I try to put on a brave face or keep busy. It just follows me around the house all day long.
Have you noticed that you feel more tired than usual or that you don’t have the energy to do even simple tasks?

Well, I wouldn't say I'm completely exhausted, no. Not like some people get when they have the flu or something dreadful like that, where they can't even lift their heads off the pillow. I mean, I'm 74, so I suppose I'm not exactly springing out of bed like a teenager anyway, but I don't feel like my energy has just entirely vanished into thin air. 

I'm still getting up, eventually, like I said, and I still manage to do the things that absolutely have to be done around the house. The dishes still get washed, eventually, and I still make sure the mail is brought in from the box at the end of the driveway, even if it takes me a little longer to get around to doing it. It's more just that... well, the desire to do them is gone, not the energy itself, if that makes any sense at all. 

Like yesterday, for instance, I needed to run the vacuum over the rug in the living room because I'd tracked in some dry grass from the yard. Now, normally I would just pull the Hoover right out of the hall closet and get it done in five minutes flat. And I knew I had the physical strength to do it—it's not a heavy machine at all, I bought one of those lightweight ones a few years back specifically so it wouldn't strain my shoulder. But I just stood there looking at the closet door, and I just couldn't bring myself to open it. It wasn't that my arms were too tired or my legs were weak... I just didn't want to. So, no, I wouldn't say it's a lack of energy, exactly. Just a lack of... well, a lack of wanting to use whatever energy I do have left.
Would you say that your mood has been low or depressed most of the time, nearly every day, rather than just occasionally feeling down?

Well, yes, I suppose I did touch on that just a moment ago, didn't I? But yes, it really is most of the time. Nearly every single day, just like you said. It's not just a passing mood, like when it rains for three days straight and you feel a bit gloomy because you can't get out into the garden. It's much more persistent than that. 

Like I was trying to explain earlier, most mornings now, I wake up and there's just this heavy, low feeling right from the start. It's as if... well, it's as if all the color has just completely drained right out of the day before I even manage to get myself dressed. And it just stays with me. I'll make my tea—Earl Grey, usually, with just a splash of milk—and I'll sit there at the kitchen table, and that heaviness is just sitting right there next to me. It doesn't seem to matter if the sun is shining beautifully outside or if the postman brings a nice letter from my sister in Ohio. The feeling just lingers and lingers, all day long, day after day. So yes, it's certainly not just an occasional thing anymore. It's become quite a constant companion, I'm afraid, and not a very pleasant one at that.
How long have you been feeling this way, with the heaviness and loss of interest in your usual activities?

Well, let me think back... it's not always easy to pinpoint an exact day, is it? Because these things, they sort of creep up on you like a slow leak in a tire. You don't really notice it's going flat until you're already bumping along the road. But if I really sit down and trace it back... yes, it would have been just after the new year, last year. I remember because I was taking down the holiday decorations—which I usually take such pride in, wrapping each little glass ornament in tissue paper just the way my mother taught me—and I just felt this... this profound emptiness settle in. 

So that would make it... well, goodness, it's been about a year and two months now. This low, colorless stretch has been with me for about a year and two months. I remember looking at the calendar in the kitchen—the one with the lovely painted cottages my niece always gets me for Christmas—and thinking, well, it's just the post-holiday blues, everyone gets those, don't they? You know how January can be, so awfully cold and gray, and the days are just so terribly short. You expect to feel a little bit down. 

But then February came, and March, and the weather started to turn, and I still felt just as gray inside as I did in January. And here we are, fourteen months later, and it just hasn't lifted at all. I kept waiting for it to pass, I really did. I kept telling myself to just give it another week, just keep putting one foot in front of the other and eventually the fog will clear. But a year and two months is an awfully long time to wait for the color to come back to things, isn't it? It just feels like an absolute lifetime when you're sitting in the middle of it every single day.
